rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.7 describe a 2017/2018 field experiment in a 0.5 ha nectarine orchard with control (ETc-based) vs precise deficit irrigation (PDI) triggered by capacitance-probe soil water content thresholds, four replicates per treatment. Q2: Section 3.1 and Figure 2B report irrigation measured by in-line water meters of 420.4 mm (control) vs 251.6 mm (PDI), i.e. about 40% less water; Table 1 and Section 3.3 report no significant yield difference. Q4: Sections 2.2 and 3.2, Figures 1 and 2C report the intermediate variable (soil water content in 0-0.5 m and relative extractable water, with PDI reducing REW by up to 15% postharvest and 4% in fruit growth) and Figure 3A the resulting stem water potential, i.e. the pathway by which threshold-based scheduling reduces applied water.
rows.notes: Water applied measured only with in-line water meters (one method), one site, one crop, one season, plot scale. The conclusion says the strategy could be promising in clay-loam soils in Mediterranean areas and that <U+03A8>stem must be considered to adjust soil water depletion at each phenological period, but this is framed as scope/recommendation rather than a stated requirement, so Q7 kept at no. No dispersion measure is given for the irrigation volumes (accumulated means in Fig. 2B without SE). Stated limitations concern the remote indices under moderate stress, not the water-saving result itself.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.7 describe a field experiment comparing ETc-scheduled control with sensor-based PDI in nectarine trees, four replicates. Q2: Table 1 and Section 3.3 report no significant differences between control and PDI in yield (8.37 vs 6.24 t/ha, ns), number of fruits, fruit mass and crop load, under 40% less irrigation; Section 3.5 and Conclusions repeat no yield penalty. Q4: Figures 2C and 3 and Section 3.2 measure the intermediate variables (soil water content/REW, midday stem water potential about 0.25 MPa lower in PDI, gas exchange reductions of 12-18%) that link the sensor-based deficit to crop performance. Q9: Table 1 gives yield components as means <U+00B1> SE (n = 4 replicates).
rows.notes: Single site, cultivar, soil and season; yield assessed at plot level only. The authors note yields were lower than other reports due to management practices, and that PDI did not increase crop WUE because of fewer commercial-sized fruits from higher cracking; these are explanations rather than explicit limitations of the no-yield-penalty result, so Q8 kept at no with some doubt. Note the numeric yield gap (8.37 vs 6.24 t/ha) is sizeable though non-significant with n = 4; the authors do not discuss statistical power.

notes: Full text available; figure captions and some paragraphs are duplicated/garbled by PDF extraction but all results sections and tables are readable. The study's main focus is comparing terrestrial and remote water-status indicators; the water saving and yield comparison are secondary but are the study's own measured results.
